newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian newspapers welcome Sharif's victory.
newsitem.headline: Indian newspapers welcome Sharif's victory.

text.p: Indian newspapers on Wednesday saw hope for better relations with Pakistan in Nawaz Sharif's election victory, but warned he first had to tackle serious internal problems.

"In Nawaz Sharif's impressive victory lies some hope of a durable government government in Pakistan despite the qualms which the lowest-ever voter turnout since 1988 must arouse," an editorial in The Indian Express newspaper said.
The Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by former prime minister Sharif scored a sweeping victory over arch-rival Benazir Bhutto in Monday's national election.
Pakistan President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government last November accusing it of corruption and misrule.

"With his decisive victory, Mr Sharif has squarely demolished his opponents -- not just rabble-rousing Ms Bhutto but also Mr Imran Khan, who in the end turned out to be a mere media creation," The Times of India said.
The latest result showed Sharif's party had secured 134 seats of the 202 declared in the 217-member National Asembly while Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party was straggling in with a meagre 18 seats.
"Imran Khan the cricketing hero has proved to be a political zero," an editorial in The Economic Times said. Khan failed to win in any constituency where results had been declared.
Hopes for better India-Pakistan ties dominated the editorials.
"For India, Mr Sharif's return to power with a majority augurs well. It will inject a measure of stability into uncertian political climate of the sub-continent," The Times of India said.
The Asian Age said Sharif, unlike Bhutto, had indicated his willingness to discuss a host of thorny bilateral issues dominated by the crisis in Kashmir.
Carved out of British India in 1947 in a bloodstained partition of the subcontinent, India and Pakistan have fought three wars, two of them over troubled the Kashmir region.
The neighbours have not held official talks for more than three years, mainly because of deep differences over Kashmir.
Pakistan has said it wants Kashmiris to be able to vote in a plebiscite to determine their future. India, which rules over two-thirds of the Himalayan region, says the issue is strictly internal.
The Hindu newspaper cautioned Sharif on the dangers ahead.

"An economy in the doldrums, a deeply divided polity, collapsing law and order and civil life, self-sought tangles in external relations -- the list of crisis crying for attention can be daunting to any new democratic government," The Hindu said.
Sharif's success will depend on his ability to ward off the threat from the fundamentalists and the powerful military establishment, it added.
"Pakistan has the outer husk of democracy but lacks the kernel. It needs strong independent institutions that can withstand subversion by politicians," The Economic Times said.
